data.title: Australia flash PMI sinks to 46.1 as private sector shrinks at fastest pace in 5 years
data.description:
A drop this deep, alongside the first easing in input cost inflation for months, weakens the case for further Australian monetary tightening. That leaves the Australian dollar exposed if rate markets start pricing a gentler path. The sharp fall in new export orders also points to softening external demand, at a time when global equities are already under heavy pressure. Prices are still running above their long-run averages, though, so policymakers are unlikely to move quickly to declare inflation beaten. Traders may also treat the flash reading cautiously until the final data in early December.

---
Higher interest rates are now hitting Australian demand across the board: services have joined manufacturing in contraction, new orders are at a five-year low and confidence is draining away.

data.title: Goldman names 3 signals that could mark a bottom as the S&P 500 sits 12% below its record
data.description:
Goldman's positioning data suggests that last week's rout cleared out mainly the fast money. Mutual funds, ETF buyers and asset managers are still heavily long, which leaves room for more forced or discretionary selling before any bottom forms. A December hike is close to fully priced and no Fed pivot is in sight, so AI earnings news is the most likely of the three catalysts to change the picture. The shift toward a growth downgrade favours defensive sectors and government bonds over cyclicals. It could also weigh on demand-sensitive commodities if it persists.

---

data.title: New Zealand retail volumes jump 2.2% in Q3, more than four times the expected pace
data.description:
A beat of this size is supportive for the New Zealand dollar and should firm rate expectations at the margin, since it weakens the case that NZ consumers need more help. Any boost may be short-lived, though, with global risk appetite under heavy pressure after last week's Wall Street rout. A high-beta currency like the kiwi tends to follow broader sentiment in that kind of market. Liquidity is also thinner than usual with Tokyo closed, which can exaggerate the first move in either direction.

----

data.title: Seoul readies a market fund unused since 2008 after the Kospi sinks
data.description:
The measures give Korean stocks a policy backstop before Monday's open. Readying the fund rather than deploying it, though, leaves authorities room to hold back unless selling becomes disorderly. Looser buyback limits could help the chip heavyweights and other large caps most, since they have the cash to step in. A Bank of Korea hike on Thursday would mean tighter monetary policy while equities are falling, which could weigh on sentiment even as fiscal and regulatory authorities try to calm it. With Japan shut for a holiday, Seoul's session is likely to set the tone for Asian tech this morning, and the won will show whether foreign outflows are building.

---

data.title: US equity rout: Bessent cautions Fed against overtightening, before its December decision
data.description:
With a quarter-point hike in December close to fully priced, Bessent's comments mainly push back against the governors (well, one, looking at you Waller!) arguing for 50 basis points. They do little to dislodge 25bp as the base case. If the equity correction deepens, the bigger risk for rate markets is that a hold gets priced back in. For oil, the administration's argument depends on crude-driven inflation fading, so softer energy prices would strengthen Bessent's case and a new spike would back the hawks. Gold has tended to fall on rising hike expectations, so any easing of that pricing could take some pressure off the metal.

---

data.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia 23 November 2026. Japanese markets are closed today.
data.description:

Japanese markets are closed on Monday for Labor Thanksgiving Day. Tokyo equities and Japanese government bonds are not trading, and physical US Treasuries will not change hands in the Asian session. data.title: Bitcoin analysis: More volume, but less downside damage (possible dip?)
data.description:
Bitcoin's rebound from $55,130 has some encouraging short-term evidence behind it. Still, the broader Bitcoin outlook is not yet bullish again, and the $62,000-$62,640 area may help decide whether this is a recovery in progress or just a bounce inside a larger downtrend.

Bitcoin's rebound from $55,130 on November 21 to roughly $61,500 on November 22 is notable for more than one reason. Yes, the move was large, about 11% from low to rebound high. But the more useful clue may be what happened between trading volume and price damage.

data.title: Nasdaq 100 posts worst week since March 2020
data.description:
U.S. stocks closed sharply lower Friday, with the Nasdaq 100 falling 5.61% on the day and 10.43% for the week, its worst since March 2020. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28%, wiping out its gains for the year, while the S&P 500 dropped 3.70% for its seventh straight decline. The Dow lost 950 points.

Nvidia fell 14.01% to $125.53 after Reuters reported that the SEC was probing its accounting. The selling reached across the AI trade, from the companies designing chips to the ones supplying memory, optical gear and power. Treasuries caught a bid, with the 10-year yield down 12 basis points to 4.93%. Even with yields moving lower, tech shares remained under pressure.

data.title: AUDUSD is the biggest mover of the major currencies this week.  The price falls -2.30% for the week.
data.description:
The AUDUSD is the weakest of the major currencies vs the greenback. It fell -2.3%.  The price has now fallen for 10 consecutive days. That move has taken the price from a high on November 10 at 0.69296 to the low today at 0.6609 or -320 pips.  

The 320-pip slide in AUDUSD started with a repricing of Fed rate expectations and picked up steam as Australia’s jobs market weakened and the global equity selloff deepened. The Aussie’s 2.30% decline this week, the largest of the seven majors you tracked against the USD, also reflected weakness against other currencies, including the yen and euro.

data.title: Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran as military warns of strain. FT
data.description:
President Donald Trump is considering new strikes on Iran, the Financial Times reports, as hawkish officials in Washington and Israel urge him to resume military action.

U.S. military planners are warning that American forces risk becoming overextended if the standoff drags into the new year. The warning adds pressure on Trump as he weighs whether to restart strikes and how long U.S. forces can sustain their current posture.

data.title: Fed’s Cook says monetary policy isn’t restrictive enough
data.description:
The Fed’s Cook weighed in on inflation, the labor market and the need for tighter monetary policy in remarks that crossed the wires.

  • Fed’s current monetary policy stance is not providing needed restraint.
  • September’s interest rate hike was not enough to curtail high inflation.
  • High inflation does not give U.S. central bank space to be patient.
  • Holding off on rate hikes increases risk that inflation will embed in economy.
  • Data since September points to need for tighter monetary policy.
  • Current level of inflation is of “great concern.”
  • U.S. economic growth is strong, labor market is healthy and stable.
  • Embedded inflation will require more aggressive Fed response.
  • Financial conditions are too accommodative right now.
  • Tariff impact on inflation has faded.
  • Little evidence AI is weighing on job market so far.

data.title: NASDAQ composite is now down on the year
data.description:
The Nasdaq Composite has given back its gains for 2026. With the index down 3.21% on the day at 23,111.52, it is now 130.47 points below its 2025 closing level of 23,241.99. That puts the index down 0.56% for the year and gives buyers a clear level to get back above if they are to start to wrestle back some control.

The Nasdaq 100 is taking the biggest hit of the five major indices, down 3.56% on the day at 25,573.95. It is still up 1.28% for 2026, but the cushion over last year’s close has narrowed to 324.10 points. That leaves the Nasdaq 100 a little more than 1% away from joining the Composite in negative territory for the year.

data.title: Could Jensen Huang end up at SpaceX? Dan Ives thinks he could work alongside Elon Musk
data.description:
SpaceX has already lined up about $40 billion in financing for AI computing equipment, including next-generation Nvidia chips.

In a Bloomberg interview about 30 minutes ago, tech analyst Dan Ives was asked where Jensen Huang might be a year from now. His answer was SpaceX. Ives floated the possibility that the Nvidia co-founder could become co-CEO alongside Elon Musk, framing it as his personal prediction.

data.title: Gold breaks below the 50% midpoint. Can buyers hold the old breakout area?
data.description: Gold is under pressure again today, with the price trading near $3,550.21 after reaching a low of $3,514.65 on my chart. That puts the price roughly 8% lower on the week and nearly 37% below the $5,598.75 high. Expectations for a December Fed hike continue to weigh on bullion, and the selloff in AI stocks may be adding to the pressure as traders sell gold to cover losses elsewhere.
